_ext: keys below are pipeline extensions, additive to SPEC SS4
protagonist: Jess Okafor, sole growth marketer at Basecamp Crate

deliverables.text: A two-circle Venn diagram, drawn inside a rectangle representing Basecamp Crate's full reachable email universe, showing Set P and Set L with all four region counts labeled from Appendix A's data (only-P, only-L, both, and neither) -- including an explicit check of whether any one of those four regions is the empty set, and a sentence stating what it would mean for this case if it were.

A written set-notation summary stating |P|, |L|, |P intersect L|, and |P union L|, showing the inclusion-exclusion arithmetic used to compute |P union L| from |P|, |L|, and |P intersect L|, plus a subset determination -- using subset/not-subset notation -- for whether P is a subset of L, or L a subset of P, defended with the actual counts from Appendix A.

A reach-and-cost table comparing Option A (mail P union L) and Option B (mail P intersect L): recipient count, total send cost at Appendix B's flat per-recipient fee, and how each compares to Appendix B's fixed remaining budget.

An expected-net-revenue calculation for each option -- reach x conversion rate x average order value, minus total send cost -- using Appendix C's benchmark conversion-rate figures, shown step by step for both options.

A one-paragraph written recommendation, using correct set notation throughout, that names which option's expected net revenue is higher and explicitly addresses why comparing raw reach alone, without the conversion-rate difference, would have been misleading.

balance.argument_a: Option A (Cast The Net) reaches 53,100 names [MA1] -- 7.7x Option B's 6,900 -- at a total send cost of $3,186.00 [MA2], comfortably inside the $4,000 budget [MA3]. A's case is the raw-reach argument: mailing every name in either list maximizes the number of people who ever see the offer, and its sourced conversion rate [S1] is a real, published, HIGH-confidence figure -- not an authored guess. Under the case's current numbers this produces $1,741.68 in expected net revenue, genuinely competitive with, though ultimately lower than, Option B's figure (see margin below) -- and A's case strengthens directly if a Hero successfully argues the intersection segment's conversion lift (MA4) is smaller than assumed.
balance.argument_b: Option B (Mail The Middle) reaches only 6,900 names [MA1], but each name shows two independent signals of interest (a recent purchase AND a newsletter opt-in), and real published research on targeting/segmentation [S1]/[S2]/[S3] supports a meaningfully higher conversion rate for this kind of segment -- modeled here at 0.60% [MA4], a deliberately moderate 3.75x lift over the sourced 0.16% broad rate. At a total send cost of only $414.00 [MA2], B produces $1,987.20 in expected net revenue -- higher than A's -- despite mailing 7.7x fewer names. B's real case is exactly the reach-vs-rate trade-off the naive comparison misses: a much smaller list can still win on expected revenue if its conversion lift is large enough to outweigh the reach gap.
balance.margin_basis: margin = |expected_net_revenue(winner) - expected_net_revenue(loser)| / expected_net_revenue(loser) x 100, where ENR(option) = reach(option) x conversion_rate(option) x AOV - reach(option) x per_recipient_cost (the corpus's standard margin formula, per skills/case-readiness/scripts/tier2_probes.py). reach(A) = |P union L| = 21,400 + 38,600 - 6,900 = 53,100 (Appendix A, inclusion-exclusion). reach(B) = |P intersect L| = 6,900 (Appendix A). ENR(A) = 53,100 x 0.0016 x 58 - 53,100 x 0.06 = 4,927.68 - 3,186.00 = $1,741.68 (loser). ENR(B) = 6,900 x 0.006 x 58 - 6,900 x 0.06 = 2,401.20 - 414.00 = $1,987.20 (winner). margin = |1,987.20 - 1,741.68| / 1,741.68 x 100 = 245.52 / 1,741.68 = 14.1%. This is within the SPEC SS2 target 10-15% band and the approved concept's 8-15% margin target. NOTE: reach(A)/reach(B) [MA1], the per-recipient cost [MA2], the intersection conversion rate [MA4], and the AOV [MA5] are all stated Modeling Assumptions, not sourced figures (only the 0.16% broad-send conversion rate [S1] is a real, sourced value) -- this margin is a designed property of the assumptions' chosen values, not an empirical finding.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Full reachable email universe (U), Set P size, Set L size, and overlap P ∩ L
modeling_assumptions.basis: No source publishes any specific company's internal CRM list sizes -- this is proprietary operational data, not a publishable dataset at any confidence grade. Chosen to reflect a realistic relative pattern for a small subscription-box company: an all-time newsletter list larger than a rolling 90-day purchaser list, with partial (not total) overlap, since the two lists were built by different vendors at different times.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Several of these counts are load-bearing -- a defensible challenge to any one of them could change which option comes out ahead. See sensitivity_disclosure[] for which specific counts, flexed +/-50%, actually flip the case's own recommendation.

modeling_assumptions.basis: No source publishes an exact blended per-recipient cost for a coordinated email-plus-paid-sync send charged against an ad budget. Set above published bare email-service-provider marginal costs (roughly $0.001/email at typical ESP overage pricing) and below typical third-party list-rental costs (roughly $0.10-$0.40/name), reflecting a company mailing its own list at a coordinated, ad-budget-funded rate.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: This figure affects both options' total cost and how close Option A comes to exceeding Appendix B's budget. See sensitivity_disclosure[] for whether flexing it +/-50% changes which option wins.

modeling_assumptions.basis: This is the case's own stated scenario detail -- Basecamp Crate's specific remaining ad budget is a constructed, disclosed detail of this fictional company, not a figure any public source could publish.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Does not change which option's expected net revenue is higher on its own in this case's current numbers (both options fit under $4,000), but a smaller budget could rule an option out entirely regardless of its expected-revenue math.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Placed-order rate for the intersection (multi-signal) segment
modeling_assumptions.basis: No source measures conversion rate for exactly 'recent purchaser AND newsletter subscriber'. Informed by three real, cited findings: Klaviyo's 2026 benchmark data showing automated/behavior-triggered sends convert at 2.11% vs. 0.16% for broad campaigns [S1] (~13x gap); HubSpot's published guidance that a properly segmented send should outperform a broadcast by 'at least 20-30%' [S2]; and Mailchimp's segmentation study finding a 100.95% higher click-through rate for segmented campaigns [S3] (clicks, not purchases). 0.60% (a 3.75x lift over the sourced 0.16% rate) is a deliberately moderate point within the real range these sources bracket -- well below Klaviyo's most extreme measured gap, since a static overlap segment and a behavior-triggered flow are not the same mechanism.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: This is the single assumption the case's recommendation is most sensitive to. See sensitivity_disclosure[] for the confirmed +/-50% flip finding.

modeling_assumptions.basis: No source publishes Basecamp Crate's own AOV. Informed by Shopify's own (Dynamic-Yield-sourced) 2025 AOV benchmarks: beauty & personal care $15-$90, apparel & accessories $40-$170, global ecommerce baseline ~$145 [S4]. Basecamp Crate is modeled as a lower-price-point outdoor-gear box, so $58 sits within the lower beauty/personal-care band and well below the global baseline, consistent with commonly observed public subscription-box price points (~$30-70/month).
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Changes the expected-revenue gap between the two options proportionally on both sides. See sensitivity_disclosure[] for the confirmed +/-50% flip finding.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: Set P's exact size is Basecamp Crate's own proprietary CRM data -- the true value exists and is knowable in principle to the company but is not publicly accessible or published anywhere, and this case's value is a documented estimate chosen to reflect a realistic 90-day purchaser list for a small subscription business. Tier 2 P5 found +50% flexes this dial and flips the verdict to A (5.0% margin, thin flip).

Set L's exact size is Basecamp Crate's own proprietary CRM data, not publicly accessible, and this case's value is a documented estimate for an all-time newsletter list at a small subscription business. Tier 2 P5 found +50% flexes this dial and flips the verdict to A (16.3% margin).

The overlap between two internal CRM lists is proprietary operational data no public source could ever publish for a real company, let alone a fictional one -- this case's value is a documented estimate. Tier 2 P5 found -50% flexes this dial and flips the verdict to A (46.4% margin, also breaches the 20% cap).

No public source publishes a blended per-recipient cost for a coordinated email-plus-paid-distribution send charged against an ad budget -- the true figure exists in principle (Basecamp Crate's actual vendor invoices) but is not publicly accessible, and this case's $0.06 value is a documented estimate bounded by real published bare-ESP and list-rental cost ranges (see modeling_assumptions[MA2]). Tier 2 P5 found -50% flexes this dial and flips the verdict to A (34.2% margin, also breaches the 20% cap).

No public benchmark measures conversion rate for exactly a recent-purchaser-and-newsletter-subscriber overlap segment -- the true figure would exist for a real campaign but is not publicly published for any company, and this case's 0.60% value is a documented estimate informed by three real cited studies (S1-S3, see modeling_assumptions[MA4]). Tier 2 P5 found -50% flexes this dial and flips the verdict to A (54.8% margin, also breaches the 20% cap) -- this is the single most flip-sensitive dial in the case, consistent with modeling_assumptions[MA4].sensitivity.

No public source publishes Basecamp Crate's own average order value -- the true figure exists in principle but is not publicly accessible for this fictional company, and this case's $58 value is a documented estimate bounded by real cited subscription-commerce AOV ranges (see modeling_assumptions[MA5]). Tier 2 P5 found +50% flexes this dial and flips the verdict to A (24.2% margin, also breaches the 20% cap).
